from.target: Earth turns, and that is what makes day and night
essentialFacts: Earth makes one full spin every day.
When your side faces the Sun it is day.
When your side turns away it is night.
The Sun is not the one moving across the sky.
from.aiExample: Stand up and turn around slowly. Face the lamp and say 'day.' Keep turning until the lamp is behind you and say 'night.' You moved. The lamp never did.
from.mapping: Your body is Earth. The lamp is the Sun. Turning your own body shows that the change comes from you, not from the light going anywhere.
from.scaffoldStarter: I turn toward the lamp: ____. I turn away from the lamp: ____.
scaffoldSteps: Pick something bright to be the Sun.
Turn your body all the way around one time.
Say 'day' and 'night' at the right moments.
coachPrompts: In your turn, what moved: you or the lamp?
from.studentPrompt: Make your own turning motion for day and night.
from.reasoningPrompt: How does turning your body help you remember why the sky changes?

hookFact.text: The Sun does not really walk across the sky. You are the one who is moving.

from.target: The Moon shines with light it borrows from the Sun
essentialFacts: The Moon does not make its own light.
Light from the Sun lands on the Moon and bounces to your eyes.
The Moon can sometimes be seen in the daytime.
from.aiExample: Picture a mirror on a wall. A mirror is not a lamp. But it can still fill a room with light, because light bounces off it. The Moon is the mirror. The Sun is the lamp.
from.mapping: Every kid has watched a mirror bounce light. So it carries the one idea that matters. The Moon is bright without being a light of its own.
from.scaffoldStarter: The Moon is like a ____, and the Sun is like a ____.
scaffoldSteps: Think of something shiny that has no light inside it.
Say where its light comes from.
Say the same thing about the Moon.
coachPrompts: If the Sun went out, what would happen to the Moon's glow?
from.studentPrompt: Make your own picture for a thing that shines with borrowed light.
from.reasoningPrompt: Why is a mirror a better match for the Moon than a candle is?

hookFact.text: You can see the Moon in the daytime too. Look for a pale white curve up in the blue.

from.context: Your class has sidewalk chalk and a sunny paved spot outside. You can go out three times in one day: morning, the middle of the day, and late afternoon.
from.audience: The kindergarten class, who will come outside to look at your chalk marks
from.drivingQuestion: Stand in the very same spot three times in one day. Will your shadow stay in the same place? Will it stay the same size?
from.seedDirection: Stand on the same X every time. If you move your feet, you will not know if the shadow moved or you did.
lockedLessonFacts: Earth makes one full spin every day.
Earth turns you toward the Sun at sunrise and away from it at sunset.
The Sun is not the thing that moves across the sky.
Day and night come in the same order every time, which makes a pattern.
openQuestions: Will your shadow be longer in the morning, or in the middle of the day?
Which way will your shadow point when you come back out?
How will you make sure you stand in the same place each time?
stakeholders: The kindergarten class who will visit your marks
Your partner who traces while you stand still
The teacher who takes you outside on time
criteria: Your feet are on the same chalk X all three times
You draw or say your guess before the first tracing
Each shadow is traced, with the time of day on it
You use the word pattern or the word spin when you tell what happened
constraints: Nobody looks straight at the Sun
from.deliverable: A chalk drawing on the ground. Three traced shadows, each with its time. And one sentence you tell the visiting class: what changed, and why.
